Extremely fun game, ruined by its community. Let me explain: The fun in this game is learning, and growing your characters and items in level. The fun isn't in BEING level 100 with level 100 gear. The fun is in PROGRESSIVELY GETTING THERE. But the community is all about boosting, which can give you 30+ levels in an hour, and gifting high level (sometimes hacked) items. So instead of experiencing the joy of progressively getting there, increasing this and that, instead you are suddenly propelled to new heights. And while that boost seems great at the very moment it happened, this pleasure is infinitely short-lived.

This is the reason I created my group, Dungeon Defenders Hardcore, for players that care about having fun with the game, not just reaching level 100 ASAP. What then? You know?

Other than that, this is an awesome game, and I am looking forward to Dungeon Defenders 2.

EDIT: DD2 was a major fail, but Trendy (named Chromatic Games now) have begun work on Dungeon Defenders: Awakened, which they promise to deliver more of what made THIS game awesome. It's even still time to fund them on their kickstarter page.

I played this game so much in 2012 back on the xbox 360 and its awesome that it still sees updates. i bought it again for the nostalgia not really thinking it would hold up to games from 2024 but i was heavily surprised that ive had more fun on this than most games ive played recently.

I was and still am a fan of DD1, it has been my favourite game since it came out on PlayStation. Collectively I wouldn't be surprised if I had over 5k hours across platforms/accounts.

Most of these hours have been on this account within the last several years. Starting out casually playing the game until strangers join me and tell me better ways to do things. After 1k hours and only after I reached level 100 with my first character did I start joining late-game lobbies and REALLY learned how to play and farm for late-game. Copying builds I witnessed in-game and recreating them in different ways was my method of learning.

I was sad when the original game was no longer going to receive any updates, but I also believe it ended in a good place. The True Boss Rush was an excellent challenge and a great way to wave goodbye to any more updates.

Then Redux happened!
The biggest thing Redux added was a new difficulty that made all maps farm-able again. Deeperwell(the first map) is decent for early-game experience and an introduction to a new enemy! While still not the best armour farm on redux, all ascension difficulty survivals had similar or better drop rates then the best maps previously on nightmare difficulty.
Redux adds new towers, new maps, new items(more accessory sets), and buffs to a lot of towers... more options... More Quality of Life changes I didn't know DD1 needed until I tried it~ (Like a built-in emulator that allows you to hide your splitscreen characters!)

There are still some things I dislike about what redux added, of course dislikes are bound to happen:
•2 pets were added as the best tower pets in the game, rendering all other options pointless. Previously any ++ pet you obtained had a chance to be good for towers, now there are only 2 'best' options.
•I was never a fan of the alternate way of getting armour, more-so because of how easy it was to obtain and target farm. While it was slowed down considerably through updates, I still think running the assault 2 DLC map over and over again without even leaving the spawn area for hours and hours is pretty lame and boring.

But those are kinda small to the whole of what redux is. There are many DPS pets that are good for many different situations, new meta is still being figured out and will need to be figured out again with the new update yet to arrive!

I chose to look forward to the new changes and will continue to enjoy the game in my own way.

Dungeon Defenders, despite its age, does not just rely on nostalgia to make it a good game. Even if you have never played it before, it can still provide a very enjoyable experience to any age group. If you want a casual game that can provide many hours of fun and enjoyment without taking things too seriously, this is a great game to dive into. On the other hand, if you're a meta-loving high end efficiency gamer, this game also offers a large level of optimization that will keep hardcore players coming back to optimize and perfect runs and builds while grinding out good items. The monetization is done right, in the form of DLC and skins, unlike its successor, Dungeon Defenders 2, which is a downright shadow of a game compared to this.

However, while there are many goods, there are also some negatives that may be considered as well. While certainly not as grindy as a game such as RuneScape, this game has a LOT of grinding. You will farm for a long time to get levels and better items, especially in the end game. If running the same level dozens of times over for hours on end to move into the next stage of progression sounds like something you don't want to do, then don't get this game unless you plan on playing very casually. 
Another negative is the end game. While there is a large amount of high tier modifiers, the majority of these will be outright skipped, as the jump from the Transcendent to Ultimate modifiers can be made by immediately getting to certain maps, like Moon Base. The modifiers in-between these frankly seem to be so rare so to be irrelevant and there is no real sense of progression through them, but rather just past them entirely. 
Finally, be aware that this game is basically over. [h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Setting & Writing[/h3]
Dungeon Defenders (DD) only has minimal story and lore. The four champions tasked with defending Etheria from the forces of evil mysteriously disappeared, and left their offspring and apprentices to helm the defense. These young but talented kids will have to use their training and wit to defend the precious Crystals from destruction across a series of locations.

[h3]Exploration & Building Phase[/h3]
Each level is a self-contained map that has one or more Eternia Crystals and various gates where mobs come from. Everything is outlined on your global map, including the precious loot chests that respawn after each wave, granting Mana (currency to build and repair traps, but also use abilities) and sometimes gear or weapons of tiered rarity depending on the difficulty. There aren’t secrets to find while exploring; the only point of combing each map is assessing its geometry to decide the best defense positions -  something you won’t always be able to do on the higher difficulties, due to the extremely annoying timer rushing waves in.

The building phase will have you position each hero’s traps as you prefer, but watch out for the defense budget which limits the total number of deployables. You can also build during battle, but in a much slower way and with the chance of being interrupted. Defenses vary from utility to barricades and damage-dealing, each hero has its own five types and they function in unique ways. Decide positions well, as defenses can’t be moved and selling them will only give back partial Mana after a wave passes.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2970603670

[h3]Combat Phase & Bosses[/h3]
Combat not only has your defenses muscling through the thick of enemies, but also sees your hero as an active component of the battle, be it with fending off enemies or supporting the defense by buffing, upgrading, repairing or replacing defenses on the go. It’s crucial that both players and defenses work together, especially at higher difficulties, so making a good build for your character is very important. The game clearly favors DPS ranged builds, which have the greatest advantage compared to melee, more exposed to deaths and consequently mana loss, or tanks which have little practical uses as defense already cover that part, and better. Many possible builds, but the meta is always raw dps at the end of the day.

Boss fights will have you fight massive HP sponges with enormous damage (and sometimes unique mechanics to stun or make them vulnerable). Their design isn’t exciting, doesn’t evolve as their HP goes down, and feels tedious due to the endlessly-spawning enemies, so solo players or smaller teams will have a hard time managing while also taking care of the boss. 

[h3]Character Progression & Crafting[/h3]
Characters level up, enabling the assignment of points to either Tower or Hero related stats, such as Heero Health, Tower Damage and many others. Equipment pieces of many different rarities, and levels, will also boost these stats significantly and can be further upgraded at the forge for a cost in Mana, which also acts as currency at the store. 

The same goes for weapons and pets: they all are mediums to give your hero better stats, and of course as in any ARPG, ‘min-maxing’ to create specialized classes that only handle combat, or defenses, is the way to go. This leads to an issue: no single hero can do it all, so you’ll have to grind multiple ones if you’re alone or with just one co-op partner, and that will take time replaying old levels again and again, otherwise you won’t be able to progress on higher settings.

Crafting involves using special materials, currencies and regular mana to improve gear, craft unique set-pieces, or enhance existing ones. It’s straightforward enough and intuitive… to a point, as there’s no clear tutorial for it and some more advanced mechanics aren’t completely clear.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2969882860

[h3]Extra Game Modes & Challenges[/h3]
The extra modes include Survival against infinite waves, Pure Strategy which removes heroes and leaves only towers, other than special challenges with unique modifiers such as moving Crystals to defend instead of static ones, to name one. They’re interesting, however most of them will have a very high level requirement.

It's well worth the time and effort. Plus, they’re still actively updating the game, so there's always something new to look forward to!

The game is still just as awesome as when I reviewed it 4 years ago. The devs have switched their focus to making the new Dungeon Defenders 2 a good game, but there's even more content coming!

There has already been one or two free community updates that have added 3 new maps. There's also another community update that's currently in beta testing. Should be out in January 2018! (Or close to it.)

Dungeon Defenders is still well worth the money. It is a great cross between Fantasy RPG and Tower Defense. This is one of my favorite games of all time.

You can start out in easy, medium, or hard mode. Any of those three should be doable at the start. Insane and Nightmare are meant for more established characters and are completely unplayable by a random starter character.

There is a campaign mode that gives you some interesting story cut scenes. I would say they are pretty good quality. Maybe not stellar, but it really fits the style of the game.

There are dozens of challenge maps in addition to the campaign maps, bonus campaign maps, Lost Eternia Shard pack, new (free community update) Lost Quests pack, and the (free community update) new release in probably Jan. 2018.

Each character has their own set of towers and / or abilities. The barbarian is the only character that can't build any towers and has to join others in order to progress. The other characters could be your own characters as you can have one or multiple builders and swap between characters at will during wave breaks. Be warned that the EV and Huntress towers / traps can't protect against flyers. You don't encounter them in the first couple of maps, but flyers are introduced fairly quickly. Really, it's quite fun to play any of the characters, but I've recently been having a blast with the Jester. The Jester has 2 base towers and random present towers that can be one tower from any other character class. The presents are tiered and Can Spawn an Ogre. This can really screw you up when you're relatively new. So, be careful when placing the presents.

Armor can be worn by any character, but has multiple tiers that require a certain level to use. Max character level is 100.

Accessories can be worn by any character and have the same tier system as armor.

Weapons are character class specific and have the same tier system. Some classes can use multiple types of weapons. If memory serves, EV uses Huntress and Apprentice weapons. Jester can use Any Weapon, which is pretty cool. Though, the Jester doesn't have any of the special combat skills that the other classes have.

"Pets" can be used by any class, but again have the same tier system as all the rest of items / equipment. There are attack, Defense, Combat, Healing, and "builder" pets. They all have thier uses and are quite fun to play with.

Bosses -- Some Bosses will be perferred to have at least one hero boost monk in the party. Hero boost on a monk, makes everyone uber awesome. Like 2 to 4x awesome. xD Though, a Monk isn't necessary as the DPS hero, it's a good choice to make as a DPS hero.

There is so much in this game, strategy, action and story. You can focus on strategy, because well this is a Tower Defense game, but you aren't forced to. You can treat it like a casual hack and slash, just don't get in the way of people building. They will love you, if you help plug holes in their defense, tank a boss, etc. The game can be as hard or as easy as you want. (With a few exceptions, easy isn't easy in some cases, but those are much newer maps.)

I suggest playing up to and including that DLC, on Nightmare if you wish, but no further, if you want to remember the game on a high note.

The last part of the DLC introduces an overpowered enemy type that ordinary defenses simply cannot fight - but of course, the minions from the paid Summoner character can. The Series-EV also becomes mandatory after a certain point, or rather, her buff beam does. And eventually, there is only one kind of map build that you can really play, as the majority of towers in the game become useless. Deviate, and you will die.
The community devs sadly doubled down on this with everything they added, and also made things like tower-stacking-exploits or the use of virtual controllers (to get more loot, map rewards and to misuse them as dummys for tower-buffing-pets) all but mandatory. Which is a shame because some of those later maps would be interesting battlegrounds.
